01 — Three directions

Three genuinely different
visual registers.

Each direction answers the same brief — a warm botanical US clean beauty brand at the $80–$300 tier for Sloane Mitchell — from a completely different emotional and typographic starting point. Direction A is the most immersive and ingredient-led. Direction B is the most elevated and heritage-adjacent. Direction C is the most restrained and modern.

The direction name is the designer's internal reference — the concept. The vibe word is what the moodboard communicates emotionally. One describes what it is. The other describes what it feels like.

What all three share: Warm, earthy palette anchored in cream and sage · Cormorant Garamond or DM Sans at display level · ingredient transparency as a structural design element, not a footnote · photography that shows texture, natural light, and linen or stone surfaces · glass packaging as a design assumption · priced without apology.

Feeling
Walking into a glass greenhouse at dawn — warm light through condensation, the smell of earth and green things, a botanist's workbench. Immersive, specific, and rooted in the natural world. The deep forest green header and cream body communicate that the brand comes from somewhere — a place with soil and seasons. The warmth score from the Tatcha audit (5/5) gets answered here.
Who it appeals to
Sloane Mitchell exactly — a buyer who connects with the origin of ingredients, who photographs the product on her linen shelf, who reads ingredient origin as part of the ritual. Appeals to the buyer who wants to know where things come from. Also appeals to the sustainability-conscious buyer who sees botanical sourcing as an ethical commitment. Strongest connection to the "ingredient literacy" behaviour identified in Step 5.
The risk
Can drift into "wellness brand" territory if not anchored by premium design execution. The botanical register is the most common direction in clean beauty — from Youth to the People to Herbivore, many brands are already here. Verdana must execute it at a level of typographic and photographic quality that makes it impossible to confuse with a $30 product. The details carry everything.

BOTANICAL ATELIER
DM Mono · ingredient labels
Heritage detail · warm amber palette
"Formulated from a single
bakuchiol harvest. Cold-pressed
within 48 hours of picking.
Nothing added. Nothing removed."
Feeling
A 19th-century Parisian apothecary that has been operating continuously and quietly for a hundred years. Deep, warm, amber-lit, deliberate. The terracotta and dark brown palette with gold accents communicates heritage, craft, and the kind of specificity that comes from decades of repetition. Ritual over routine. Each product feels like it has a story that predates the brand.
Who it appeals to
The Sloane buyer who buys on the founder story — who responds to "formulated from a single harvest" and "cold-pressed within 48 hours." Appeals to the buyer who wants heritage narrative alongside ingredient specificity. Also appeals to buyers who find Direction A too earthy and want something more refined and elevated. The gold accent reads as luxury at the visual level without requiring a gold product to execute it.
The risk
The dark warm palette and gold detail can drift toward "looks expensive, is it clean?" territory — the opposite of the trust problem Verdana is trying to solve. The apothecary aesthetic carries connotations of complexity and inaccessibility that the Sloane buyer may read as a barrier. The palette requires rigorous ingredient-forward copy to counterbalance the visual richness, or the brand starts to look like it is hiding the formula behind the aesthetic.

The formula.
Nothing else.
DM Mono · ingredient labels
Ingredient statement · minimal on cream
5% BAKUCHIOL
2% SQUALANE
0.5% PHYTOL
NOTHING ELSE
Feeling
A single product on a marble windowsill. Morning light. Nothing else in the frame. Maximum restraint — the formula is the design. The pared-back palette (cream, stone, sage, ink) strips away every decorative element and lets the ingredient statement carry the full visual weight. It is the aesthetic of a brand that has so much confidence in its formula that it does not need packaging theatre to justify the price.
Who it appeals to
The Sloane buyer who is design-literate enough to read extreme restraint as extreme quality. The buyer who uses Linear and Notion and reads nothing as everything. Also appeals to the ingredient-obsessed buyer who finds botanical imagery distracting — she wants to see the percentage, not the flower it came from. Narrower audience than A, but higher-intent — this buyer is exactly Sloane at her most discerning.
The risk
The most minimal direction is the most difficult to execute and the easiest to mistake for generic. Without exceptional photography and typography discipline, Direction C reads as "nothing" rather than "everything." It also risks being too cold for a category where warmth is Verdana's differentiator — the cream palette rescues it from clinical white, but only just. The margin for error is very thin.

05 — Selecting a direction

Which direction
earns the brief.

Generate all three moodboards using the Midjourney prompts above. Upload the images to the drop zones — they will embed automatically. Then select a direction. The selected direction becomes the locked visual system for Steps 8–13.

The recommendation — if the choice is difficult
Direction A (Botanical/Verdure) is the most directly responsive to the research. The Step 6 audit confirmed that warmth is the universal gap — every competitor scores low on W. Direction A scores highest on warmth, is most distinctive against the competitor set, and most directly addresses Sloane's B01 behaviour (discovers on TikTok via texture and origin content). Direction B is the most premium but risks obscuring ingredient transparency behind heritage aesthetics. Direction C is the most modern but the narrowest in appeal and the hardest to execute without losing warmth. For a brand whose differentiator is warm botanical transparency, Direction A has the clearest path from research to execution. That said — this is your decision, not mine.
